devices/admin/device-policy-resolution:
Device policy resolution framework

Starting with Android 14, multiple device policy management agents can set policies using DevicePolicyManager APIs.

General principles

In cases where more than one device policy management agent enforces policies over a user:

  • Device policy management agents can query the enforced or resolved policy for any policy they are able to set.
  • Every policy set results in a callback (onPolicySetResult) indicating either that the policy was set correctly or failed to set for a given reason (such as a policy conflict or hardware failure).
  • If the resolved state of a policy changes later, a callback (onPolicyChanged) is received indicating if the policy matches what that agent set.
  • Most policies operate on a strictest-win basis. This means that the strictest policy chosen by any device policy management agent gets enforced.
Note: The policies available to a device policy management agent are contingent upon the Android role held by the agent (device policy management app). Policies not listed here are supported by only one management agent, so don't present a conflict scenario.

Android 14 (API level 34) and higher

In Android 14 (API level 34) and higher, Android-compatible devices must implement the policy resolution mechanism as defined in the following table to resolve conflicts when a policy is set by more than one device policy management agent. The resolution mechanisms referenced in the following table (MostRecent, MostRestrictive, StringSetUnion, and TopPriority) are class names of the resolution mechanisms defined in the Android Open Source Project.

Policies identified by PolicyIdentifier instances document their resolution strategy individually in their API reference documentation.

DevicePolicyManager API Resolution mechanism
  • setPermittedInputMethods
  • getPermittedInputMethods
 MostRecent: The most-recent policy is enforced when set by multiple admins.
  • setUninstallBlocked
  • isUninstallBlocked
  • setCameraDisabled
  • getCameraDisabled
  • setApplicationHidden
  • isApplicationHidden
  • setAccountManagementDisabled
  • getAccountTypesWithManagementDisabled
  • setAutoTimeRequired
  • addUserRestriction
  • addUserRestrictionGlobally
  • clearUserRestriction
  • getUserRestrictions
  • setScreenCaptureDisabled
  • getScreenCaptureDisabled
 MostRestrictive: Sets the user restriction if any admin has set it.
  • setUserControlDisabledPackages
  • getUserControlDisabledPackages
 StringSetUnion: Resolves as the union of policies set by one or more admins (for policies represented as a Set of Strings).
  • setLockTaskFeatures
  • getLockTaskFeatures
  • getLockTaskPackages
  • setLockTaskPackages
  • addPersistentPreferredActivity
  • clearPackagePersistentPreferredActivities
 TopPriority: Resolves with the following most-to-least priority order defined by the role held by the device policy management agent:
  1. The device lock admin
  2. The enterprise admin
  3. Any other admin

Audio frequency tests

The audio frequency CTS-V tests require human intervention and some external hardware, including an audio loopback dongle, a USB reference microphone, and external speakers.

To access the tests on this page, see General instructions.

Run the audio frequency line test

This test uses an audio loopback dongle to characterize the left and right line audio output from the 3.5 mm analog jack. The test uses the mic feedback from the plug to capture audio and compute a frequency response for each channel.

A criterion for minimum energy expected in each band (out of four) is applied for each channel.

To run this test:

  1. Follow the General instructions to access the test.

  2. Tap Yes or No to report whether the device has a physical headset port. If it doesn't have a physical port, mark the test as passed by tapping the green checkmark at the bottom of the screen.

    Figure 1. Audio frequency line.

  3. Connect a loopback plug to the headset connector (see Audio loopback plug).

  4. Tap Loopback Plug Ready.

    Figure 2. Loopback plug ready.

  5. Tap Test and wait for the test to complete.

  6. When the test is complete, view the results on the test screen.

    Figure 3. Testing complete.

  7. If the test passed, tap the green checkmark. If the test failed, tap !.

Run the audio frequency speaker test

This test uses the signal captured by an external USB reference microphone to assess the speakers' frequency response.

A reference microphone delivers a flat, uncolored audio response. These microphones are often used for analysis and measurement equipment.

A reference microphone has the following minimum recommended characteristics:

  • Flat frequency response on range 100 Hz to 20 kHz: +/- 2 dB S/N ratio 70 dB (A-weighted)
  • THD ratio at 1,000 Hz less than 1% at 127 dB SPL

Recommended microphones include the miniDSP USB measurement calibrated microphone and the Dayton Audio UMM-6 USB measurement microphone.

Note: Run this test in a quiet room.

To run the test:

  1. Tap Yes or No to report whether the DUT supports a connection of a USB reference microphone. If it doesn't, mark the test as passed by tapping the green checkmark at the bottom of the screen.

    Figure 4. Support USB microphone.

  2. Connect a USB reference microphone to the DUT and place the microphone 20 cm away from the DUT and perpendicular to the center of the screen:

    Figure 5. Device under test.

  3. Tap USB Reference microphone ready.

    Figure 6. Microphone ready.

  4. Tap Test and wait for the test to complete.

  5. When the test is complete, view the results on the test screen.

  6. If the test passed, tap the green checkmark. If the test failed, tap !.

Run the audio frequency microphone test

This test requires both external speakers for a white noise sound source and a USB reference microphone to calibrate the DUT's internal microphone against. The speakers don't need to have a flat frequency response, but they need good coverage from low frequencies (100 Hz) to high frequencies (20 kHz).

Note: Run this test in a quiet room.

To run the test:

  1. Report whether the DUT has a physical audio output port. If it doesn't, mark the test as passed by tapping the green checkmark at the bottom of the screen.

    Figure 7. Audio microphone test.

  2. Position the speakers 40 cm perpendicular to the center of the screen of the DUT.

    Figure 8. Device under test.

  3. Connect external speakers to the auxiliary phone using the headphone or line out connector. Unplug any USB microphone connected to the DUT.

  4. Tap Play on the auxiliary phone, tap Test on the DUT, and wait for the test to complete.

    Figure 9. Test noise.

  5. Connect a USB reference microphone to the DUT. Keep the external speakers connected and position the microphone next to the DUT's internal microphone, pointed toward the external speakers.

    Figure 10. Device position.

    Figure 11. Microphone position.

  6. Tap Test on the DUT to test USB background and wait for the test to complete.

    Figure 12. Test USB background.

  7. Tap Play on the auxiliary phone, tap Test on the DUT, and wait for the test to complete.

    Figure 13. Test USB noise.

  8. Record the test results.

Run the audio frequency unprocessed test and voice recognition test

This test requires a sound pressure level (SPL) meter in addition to a USB reference microphone and external speakers.

For the frequency unprocessed test, if the DUT has a definition for the audio frequency unprocessed feature, all sections of this test must pass. If the DUT doesn't define this feature, the test can pass even if some sections fail.

Note: Run this test in a quiet room.

To run the test:

  1. Connect external speakers to the auxiliary phone. Unplug any USB microphone connected to the DUT.

  2. To conduct the tone test:

    1. Tap Play on the auxiliary phone.

    2. Move the SPL meter back and forth in a straight line from the speakers until it detects a sound pressure level of 94 dB SPL for the frequency unprocessed test and 90 dB SPL for the frequency voice recognition test. The following figures illustrate the sound pressure level shown on the sound pressure level meter:

      Figure 14. Test tone setup for preset unprocessed.

      Figure 15. Test tone setup for preset voice recognition.

    3. Move the DUT and place the microphone in about the same location found in the previous step.

      Figure 16. SPL meter placement.

    4. Tap Play on the auxiliary phone.

    5. Tap Test on the DUT. The DUT performs a short audio capture.

      Figure 17. Audio capture.

  3. To conduct the noise test:

    1. Position the speakers perpendicular to the center of the screen of the DUT and 40 cm away.

      Figure 18. Speaker placement.

    2. Tap Play on the auxiliary phone.

    3. Tap Test on the DUT and wait for the test to complete.

      Figure 19. Running test.

  4. To test USB background:

    1. Connect a USB reference microphone to the DUT and position it close to the DUT's internal microphone.

    2. Tap Test. The test runs and displays results on screen.

      Figure 20. Running test.

  5. To test USB noise:

    1. Place a USB microphone in the same position as in the previous test.
    2. Tap Play on the auxiliary phone. The speaker plays broadband noise.

    3. Tap Test on the DUT. The test runs and displays results on screen.

      Figure 21. Running test.

  6. View the results for all four sections of the test. Repeat sections as needed.

    Figure 22. Test results.

  7. If the test passed, tap the green checkmark. If the test failed, tap !.

Cuttlefish: Restart and reset

This page describes how to restart and reset Cuttlefish virtual devices. Resetting a Cuttlefish device to its initial disk state is referred to as powerwashing in the command line tool.

When running automated or manual workflows with multiple different procedures, such as test suites, resetting the Cuttlefish device between procedures ensures that the behavior of each procedure is independent. If the disk state isn't reset, one procedure can affect the behavior of the following procedure.

The restart and reset procedures described on this page assumes that you have created a Cuttlefish device and have set some state on the disk.

# Launch a device
launch_cvd
# Make some modifications to the device
adb shell touch /storage/self/primary/Documents/hello
# Check the device state
adb shell ls /storage/self/primary/Documents

From this starting point, you can use the following restart and reset flows:

  • If device is responsive, perform a clean restart using adb reboot.
  • If device is unresponsive, perform an unclean restart using restart_cvd.
  • Reset the device state using powerwash_cvd.
  • Stop the device and change the launch_cvd arguments while keeping the device state or forcibly clearing the device state.

Cuttlefish quick reset implementation

Cuttlefish uses a quick reset implementation that's dependent on protecting the disks behind qcow2 disk overlays. By default, Cuttlefish treats original disks as read-only and uses overlays to capture disk writes.

However there are drawbacks to using copy-on-write overlays. Notably, external changes to the underlying disks break compatibility with existing overlays, and cause an inconsistent disk state. Cuttlefish forcibly recreates the overlays when it detects incompatible changes.

Forcibly recreating the overlays is undesirable when developing a feature that requires keeping part of the disk in a particular initialized state while swapping out a different part of the disk. For example, installing an app with a particular user configuration and then repeatedly swapping out the kernel to test the interaction between the app and different kernel builds. In this case, it might be worth disabling the overlays.

Reset devices

The following sections describe ways to reset a Cuttlefish device to its initial disk state.

Reset one device

To reset one Cuttlefish device to its initial disk state, run:

powerwash_cvd

powerwash_cvd shuts down the virtual machine, resets any changes made to the virtual machine disk, restarts the virtual machine, and waits until it finishes booting. The instance preserves the original flags given to launch_cvd.

In a multi-tenant configuration, powerwash_cvd restarts a single instance out of the instance group:

powerwash_cvd --instance_num=N

Reset all devices

To stop and reset one or more devices to their initial disk states, run:

stop_cvd
launch_cvd --resume=false

stop_cvd performs an unclean shutdown and stops the device.

Adding --resume=false to launch_cvd makes Cuttlefish destroy all files related to the previously running instance before starting the next run. It's safe to add any additional launch_cvd flags.

In a multi-tenant configuration,ß stop_cvd shuts down the entire instance group.

Restart devices

The following sections describe ways of restarting a device without resetting the device to its initial disk state.

Clean restart

To do a clean restart of the device when the device is responsive, run:

adb reboot

adb reboot takes the device through the full shutdown procedure, syncing changes to the disk and making sure processes shut down. Cuttlefish host processes aren't involved. This procedure could be unavailable if the device has entered a bad state and become unresponsive.

To do a clean restart of a single Cuttlefish device in a multi-tenant configuration, specify the serial number of the target device when running adb-reboot. If no target device is specified, adb doesn't restart any device.

adb -s SERIAL reboot

Unclean restart

Note: An unclean restart is when a device is instantly shut down without ensuring changes to the disk are synced when processes are shut down.

To perform an unclean restart when the device is unresponsive, run:

restart_cvd

restart_cvd performs an unclean shutdown by instantly shutting down the Cuttlefish device. restart_cvd is the equivalent of disconnecting and reconnecting the battery to a physical device. Disk writes might not persist if they were in progress. restart_cvd waits until the device has fully booted again before exiting.

In a multi-tenant configuration, restart_cvd restarts a single instance out of the instance group. To specify which Cuttlefish instance to restart, use the instance_num flag.

restart_cvd --instance_num=N

If --instance_num isn't used, the instance number defaults to 1.

Restart using different launch_cvd flags

To stop one or more devices and relaunch with different launch_cvd flags, run:

stop_cvd
launch_cvd NEW_FLAG

stop_cvd performs an unclean shutdown similar to restart_cvd. It leaves the device in a dormant state that can be started again later with a different launch_cvd command. As with restart_cvd, disk writes might not persist if they aren't fully synced to the disk. To safely save data to disk, run adb reboot first.

adb reboot
stop_cvd
launch_cvd NEW_FLAG

If changes to launch_cvd flags force a change to the disk layout that's incompatible with the copy-on-write implementation, launch_cvd ignores the old disk modifications and resets to the original disk state. For a full list of flags, see Flags.

Run without an overlay

To opt out of quick-reset support, run:

launch_cvd --use_overlay=false

--use_overlay=false treats the Cuttlefish disk files as read-write, and changes are propagated into those files.

Changing between --use_overlay=false and the default can cause compatibility errors. To forcibly clean up the prior device state, run:

stop_cvd
rm $HOME/cuttlefish $HOME/cuttlefish_runtime $HOME/cuttlefish_assembly

Cuttlefish can't safely navigate the transition between the flows with and without overlays, so this change deletes all the Cuttlefish management state. If external disk files are modified and are reused later together with overlays, the earlier modifications are considered part of the baseline state.

Flags

You can add arguments using flags when launching a Cuttlefish device using launch_cvd. However, for certain flags (Flags that must stay the same), data loss can occur if flags are changed between launch_cvd commands. To ensure no data loss occurs when running a sequence of commands that include launch_cvd, stop_cvd, and then launch_cvd again, use the same flags for every launch_cvd command. For example, if the first launch_cvd flag includes the argument --kernel_path=KERNEL_PATH, the second launch_cvd invocation must also include the same --kernel_path=KERNEL_PATH argument, or any file system changes made before stop_cvd are lost in the second launch_cvd invocation. The file referenced by KERNEL_PATH must also have the same contents.

Some flags are safe to change between launch_cvd invocations. The following sections list the flags that must stay the same to avoid data loss and flags that can be safely changed without data loss. For details on individual flags, refer to the source ( flags.cc , disk_flags.cc ) or run launch_cvd --help.

automotive/sdv/workstreams/telemetry/clo:
User guide

You can run simulations using the provided web demo or by calling the REST API directly.

Input and output

Input and output files use the Cloud Storage bucket from the Terraform setup.

The input directory must contain metrics_config.zip and publisher_config.zip files. You can define the path to it as required.

The bucket for outputs contains a simulations directory, which stores each simulation by its ID. Each simulation directory contains an inputs folder with the copied input files and an outputs folder. The outputs folder contains the bugreport, the logcat file, and generated simulator files.

Use the web demo

The platform includes a Flutter-based web application for demonstration purposes that lets you view, create, and manage simulations. You are encouraged to build your own user interface tailored to your needs.

The demo app is deployed to App Engine and requires you to sign in with a Google Account. This is protected using an OAuth 2.0 Client ID configured in your Google Cloud project. The signed-in account must have IAM permissions to invoke the deployed Cloud Functions. See Authorize access with IAM for instructions on granting the necessary permissions to user accounts, such as the Cloud Functions Invoker role (roles/cloudfunctions.invoker).

User workflow

  1. Sign in with your Google Account, authenticated using the OAuth 2.0 process.
  2. View simulations on the main page, which lists all simulations by querying the Firestore database, which holds all execution information.
  3. Navigate to a form to schedule a new simulation by clicking the + action button in the lower-right corner. You provide several parameters, including the input path, build ID, and instance type. For more information, see Create a simulation.
  4. Check the monitor status on the simulation list updates, which show the status of the new simulation, for example, PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETED.
  5. After a simulation completes, view the generated reports and artifacts. The input files, output reports, logs, Logcat, and Bugreports are stored in Cloud Storage.
  6. Optional: Cancel a scheduled or running simulation.

API use

For automation and integration with other systems, you can use the REST API.

The placeholder CLOUD_FUNCTION_URL used in the Authentication section and in endpoint definitions refers to the base URL of the Cloud Function being invoked. You can find function URLs in the Google Cloud console on the Cloud Functions page; the URL for each function is shown on the Trigger tab of its Function details page. Alternatively, you can find these URLs in the Terraform outputs that are printed after you run an apply command.

Authentication

All API requests must be authenticated with an identity token that proves the caller's identity. The identity (user or service account) must have Cloud Functions Invoker permissions on the target function.

  1. User invocation (local and CLI): When invoking the API from a local machine or a non-Google Cloud environment, you must use a Google-issued identity token obtained for a user account.

    TOKEN=$(gcloud auth print-identity-token)

  2. Service account invocation (within Google Cloud): When invoking the API from a Google Cloud resource (for example, a Compute Engine VM, another Cloud Function, or a Kubernetes cluster), use the identity of the resource's attached Service Account. The token should be fetched from the resource's metadata server.

    TOKEN=$(curl -s "http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/instance/service-accounts/default/identity?audience=CLOUD_FUNCTION_URL" -H "Metadata-Flavor: Google")

Include the retrieved token in the Authorization header of your requests as a Bearer token.

Endpoints

User-facing endpoints of the Cloud Telemetry Simulation stack let you create and delete simulations or read simulation information from the database.

Note: All API requests must include the Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN header as described in the Authentication section.

Create a simulation

This endpoint creates a new simulation request and schedules it for execution.

  • Endpoint: POST https://CLOUD_FUNCTION_URL/simulation-orchestrator-receive-requests

  • Request body:

    {
  "build_id": "latest",
  "file_path": "inputs/my-test-case/",
  "instance_type": "n1-standard-8",
  "owner": "user@example.com",
  "max_simulation_time": 300,
  "max_report_count": 5
}

    • build_id (string): The tag of the agent Docker image to use, for example,latest.

      Important: This must match a tag defined in the infrastructure's allowed image map, for example, latest, stable. The system rejects unknown tags if a SHA256 map is defined in Terraform.

    • file_path (string): The path within the GCS bucket to the folder containing metrics_config.zip and publisher_config.zip.

    • instance_type (string): The Compute Engine machine type. This type must support nested virtualization, such as the n1, n2, or t2d series. For more information, see the nested virtualization overview.

core/display/hagc:
Headroom Adaptive Gain Curves (HAGC)

Headroom Adaptive Gain Curves (HAGC), standardized as SMPTE ST 2094-50, is the underlying technology behind Eclipsa Video. Eclipsa Video is a modern HDR video standard that lets creators preserve the artistic intent of their content across devices and viewing environments.

Android 17 provides support for playback and capture of HAGC content.

OEM integration

The following sections describe the steps for how OEMs can integrate HAGC support into their devices.

Gralloc integration

To transport of SMPTE ST 2094-50 metadata, ensure that the gralloc Mapper HAL supports storage and retrieval of SMPTE ST 2094-50 standard metadata.

Camera integration

To capture HAGC content, ensure that the camera HAL advertises a DynamicRangeProfile indicating SMPTE ST 2094-50 metadata is attached to an output camera stream. For more details, see 10-bit camera output.

Codec integration

To decode HAGC content, ensure that codec implementations that extract T.35 messages from an input bitstream (for example, AV1 and H.265) support extracting C2StreamHdrDynamicMetadataInfo with a type of HDR_DYNAMIC_METADATA_TYPE_SMPTE_2094_50.

Display integration

To display HAGC content, ensure that the Hardware Composer (HWC) exposes least one LutProperties for hardware-accelerated tonemapping. For the best quality, implementations are recommended to expose a 3D LUT. Devices that don't support hardware-acceleration, or devices that need to validate their LUT support, may defer to a reference GPU-based tonemapping shader, by enabling the debug.sf.force_agtm_without_luts system property.

Android 17 Camera Image Test Suite release notes

The Android 17 release includes a number of changes to Camera ITS. This page summarizes the Camera ITS changes for Android 17.

Python and package versions

For Android 17 and higher, we strongly recommend using package management software to bundle the correct versions of packages to create a virtual environment for Android release development. For an example package management tool that handles most of the packages required, see the Python 3 documentation for venv.

Note: The correct Python version and FFmpeg must be installed directly as part of the initial setup. Because pip is designed solely for installing Python packages, it can't handle Python itself or external dependencies such as FFmpeg.

To create the virtual environment with venv, follow these steps:

  1. Install Python 3.14 and python3-venv

    sudo apt install python3.14
sudo apt install python3.14-venv python3.14-dev

  2. Verify python installation

    python3.14 --version

  3. Update apt and install pip

    sudo apt-get update
sudo apt install python3-pip

  4. Create a virtual environment

    python3.14 -m venv its_android17_env

  5. Activate the virtual environment

    source its_android17_env/bin/activate

  6. Create its_android17_env.txt with the list of required packages

    ImageIO==2.37.4
PyYAML==6.0.3
contourpy==1.3.3
cycler==0.12.1
fonttools==4.61.1
imagecodecs==2025.11.11
kiwisolver==1.5.0
lazy-loader==0.*
matplotlib==3.10.9
mobly==1.13.1
mobly-android-partner-tools==1.5.2
networkx==3.4.2
numpy==2.5.3
opencv-python==5.0.0.*
packaging==26.0.0
pillow==12.3
portpicker==1.6.0
protobuf<=7.37.0
psutil==5.9.4
pyparsing==3.2.3
pyserial==3.5.0

scikit-image==0.26.0

six==1.17.0

  7. Install packages listed its_android17_env.txt

    pip install -r its_android17_env.txt

  8. Install FFmpeg version 7.0.2 with ffmpeg downloader

    pip install ffmpeg-downloader
ffdl install 7.0.2

    (optional) If ffmpeg downloader doesn't work, download 7.0.2 from an online source.

  9. Verify FFmpeg installation of version 7.0.2

    ffmpeg -version

    If the FFmpeg version still isn't 7.0.2, symlink the binaries (adjust PATH based on where you save its_android17_env).

    ln -s ~/.local/share/ffmpeg-downloader/ffmpeg/ffmpeg ~/PATH/its_android17_env/bin/ffmpeg
ln -s ~/.local/share/ffmpeg-downloader/ffmpeg/ffprobe ~/PATH/its_android17_env/bin/ffprobe

  10. Verify which packages are installed

    pip freeze

  11. (Optional) Command to deactivate the environment:

    deactivate

New or updated scenes

Android 17 introduces the following scenes:

Scene Description
gen2_chart New scene that uses the test_chart_gen2 paper chart instead of tablet scenes to improve test consistency and reliability . The test_chart_gen2 is also used in scene_ip.

3 Uses ArUco markers for chart detection to improve speed and reliability. This change accommodates the wider range of FoV and distances seen in tele camera testing. Using markers bypasses the current sizing logic and optimizer issues. For more information, see scene3.
flash Tests can be run using the Gen2 rig.

New tests

Android 17 introduces the following tests:

ip test_jca_jpegr_ip Verifies that the white balance difference between JPEG_R JCA preview snapshot and captured images is within the chosen threshold.
wide_gamut test_display_p3 Verifies P3 JPEG output has an appropriate icc profile and contains more than 1 percent of colors outside of the sRGB gamut.

Refactored tests

In Android 17, the following tests are refactored to increase test coverage and group tests more logically:

Scene Test name Description
1_2 tests_param_tonemap_mode The scene1_2 version of the tests_param_tonemap_mode test is deprecated and is used only on devices running Android 16 or lower.
1_2 test_tonemap_sequence The scene1_2 version of the test_tonemap_sequence test is used only on devices running Android 16 or lower.

Separated test activities

In Android 17, for parallel testing on separate devices, the camera ITS tests are separated into two CTS Verifier activities, Camera ITS Test and Camera ITS Sensor Fusion Rig Test. The Camera ITS Sensor Fusion Rig Test activity contains the feature_combination and sensor_fusion scenes, and can be run separately in a sensor fusion test rig. Scene Test name Description

Gen2 rig updates

Android 17 the following tests have been migrated to the Gen2 rig:

Scene Test name Description
7 test_multi_camera_switch Migrated the test to gen2 rig setup to use the Gen2 chart for AE and AWB checks. This transition replaces tablet-based targets with physical charts to eliminate Moiré effects and provide a more stable, reproducible testing environment.

Before running the migrated tests, install the Gen2 rig chart introduced in Android 17. The new chart lets you run all sensor fusion tests in the Gen2 rig. For more information, see Set up the chart for testing.

New test status: PASS*

17 introduces the test status PASS* to detect marginally passing tests. For more information, see Marginally passing tests (PASS* test status).

Chart scaling improvements

Android 17 adds the chart_scaling parameter in config.yml for TEST_BED_TABLET_SCENES to handle the chart scaling issues with wider field of view (FoV) tele camera devices. For more information, see Chart scaling improvements: chart_scaling param.

New tablet for wide-gamut testing support

For Android 17 and higher, the Samsung Galaxy Tab S10 FE (both Wi-Fi and 5G models) is on the tablet allowlist. The Samsung Galaxy Tab S10 FE is approved for displaying wide-gamut test charts, as well as all other tablet-based scenes. To verify that your device is on the allowlist, use the command adb shell getprop ro.product.device to confirm the product ID matches the value listed in the following list.

    'gts10fewifi',  # Samsung Galaxy Tab S10 FE
    'gts10fe',  # Samsung Galaxy Tab S10 FE 5G

Aggregated result submission for build approvals

Android 17 introduces a process for submitting aggregated Camera ITS test results for build approval using the updated CTS Verifier APK.

The new aggregation system provides the following improvements:

  • Time savings: Eliminates the need to repeatedly rerun passing scenes on devices that share the same build fingerprint.
  • Parallel execution: Allows concurrent testing of multiple scenes across several devices, provided they share the same build fingerprint.
  • Simplified reporting: Enables aggregation of test results from multiple CTS Verifier reports (collected from different test runs or devices) into a single, unified submission.

For more information, see Submit aggregate test results.

core/perf/system-memory-budgets:
System memory budgets

In Android 17 and higher, the platform governs system process memory using two complementary Linux cgroup v2 mechanisms that work alongside the general application Memory Limiter:

  • System daemon protection floors (SystemMemoryBudgetManager with memory.min): When enabled by the com.android.server.am.system_process_memory_budgets feature flag (disabled by default in the initial Android 17 release), self-tuning cgroup v2 memory.min reservations (set to 90% of each daemon's settled resident working set and capped globally at 10% of total physical RAM) protect critical interactive daemons and shell processes (system_server, surfaceflinger, the graphics composer HAL, audioserver, cameraserver, netd, SystemUI, and the Home launcher) under memory pressure, replacing static PinnerService mlock file pinning.
  • System app memory ceilings (<memory-budget> with memory.high): Workload-calibrated cgroup v2 memory.high soft limits (typically 30 MB to 190 MB) declared in manifest files for persistent and background system apps (Bluetooth, Nfc, CalendarProvider, Traceur, MediaProvider, :PhotoPicker, NetworkStack, AppSearch, and TeleService) proactively reclaim cold file page cache and post-burst anonymous heap before global memory pressure occurs.

The following table compares the two mechanisms:

Dimension System daemon protection floors System app memory ceilings
Platform service SystemMemoryBudgetManager MemoryLimiter
Cgroup v2 control memory.min hard protection floor memory.high soft reclaim ceiling
Target processes Latency-critical interactive daemons and shell UI (system_server, surfaceflinger, composer HAL, audioserver, cameraserver, netd, SystemUI, and the Home app) Persistent and headless system apps, content providers, and background services (such as Bluetooth, Nfc, MediaProvider, NetworkStack, AppSearch, and TeleService)
Sizing model Self-tuning at run time (90% of settled working set, globally capped at 10% of total RAM) with zero per-device tuning tables Declarative <memory-budget> manifest XML attributes calibrated by RAM tier, process state, and display pixel count
Primary benefit Prevents interactive UI jank and wakeup stalls under memory pressure while replacing static PinnerService mlock file lists Continuously evicts cold one-time file cache and post-burst heap to leave more physical RAM for foreground and cached apps

For more information about <memory-budget> syntax, XML attributes, runtime APIs, and OS memory accounting, see Set app memory budgets and Understanding and troubleshooting Android memory.

Protect critical interactive daemons with SystemMemoryBudgetManager

Note: SystemMemoryBudgetManager is controlled by the com.android.server.am.system_process_memory_budgets feature flag, which is disabled by default in the initial Android 17 release. When the flag is disabled, the platform retains legacy PinnerService static mlock file pinning for config_defaultPinnerServiceFiles and config_pinnerHomePinBytes.

SystemMemoryBudgetManager keeps the processes that sit directly on the user's interactive path resident in physical RAM during memory pressure. Rather than pinning a static list of APK, ODEX, and VDEX files into memory with mlock (as PinnerService does for config_defaultPinnerServiceFiles and config_pinnerHomePinBytes), SystemMemoryBudgetManager assigns dynamic cgroup v2 memory.min floors to the following processes:

  • Core system slice (/sys/fs/cgroup/system): system_server, surfaceflinger, the graphics composer HAL, audioserver, cameraserver, and netd, plus any form-factor-specific native system or vendor daemons listed in config_systemMemoryBudgetAdditionalSystemProcesses (for example, android.hardware.perceptionhost and auracamerahal on XR devices).
  • Interactive app slice (/sys/fs/cgroup/apps): The main process of the configured SystemUI package (config_systemUi) and the main process of the current user's Home role holder.

Protecting the Home role holder alongside config_systemUi ensures coverage across all form factors. On form factors where config_systemUi is a lightweight compatibility package (such as Wear OS, where the watch face, notifications, and tiles run inside the Home app), the user-facing shell still receives full working-set protection. If the Home intent resolves to the config_systemUi package, the process is protected once. Only the main process of each package (processName == packageName) receives a protection floor, so auxiliary subprocesses (such as :screenshot) don't consume protection budget.

Self-tuning policy and three-level cgroup delegation

Because the working set of an interactive daemon varies widely across form factors and RAM capacities (for example, SystemUI uses about 45 MB on a smartwatch, 60 MB on a 6 GB phone, and 180 MB on a 16 GB phone), static per-device lookup tables are brittle. Instead, SystemMemoryBudgetManager derives floors directly from each process's own resident footprint using three constants:

Policy parameter Default value Behavior
Per-process floor 90% of settled memory.current less unmapped file cache Protects anonymous heap, slab, and hot mapped code while leaving the coldest 10% tail reclaimable so genuinely cold pages can still be evicted. Unmapped file cache (max(0, file - shmem - file_mapped) from memory.stat) is subtracted before applying the 90% ratio so boot package-scan cache or one-time asset reads don't inflate floors.
Global RAM cap 10% of total RAM (config_systemMemoryBudgetLowKb) Matches the PinnerService config_pinnerMaxPinnedMemoryPercentage guardrail. If the sum of 90% floors exceeds 10% of MemTotal, every floor is scaled down proportionally by the same factor.
Refresh cadence 1, 4, 16, and 64 s after start, then every 30 min A geometric settle series converges on each daemon's post-startup working set without hardcoding per-device warm-up delays, and a 30-minute steady-state refresh tracks gradual working-set growth and shrinkage over the device lifetime.

In the Linux cgroup v2 memory controller (mm/memcontrol.c:effective_protection), a leaf cgroup's effective memory.min protection is bounded by the memory.min configured on its parent and ancestor cgroups. Setting memory.min only on a leaf pid_<pid> directory while uid_<uid>/memory.min is 0 results in zero effective protection. Conversely, setting a flat memory.min only on the top /sys/fs/cgroup/system slice distributes unclaimed protection across all child UIDs and processes proportionally (memory_recursiveprot), allowing diagnostic or secondary processes sharing uid_1000 (android.uid.system) to siphon protection away from surfaceflinger and audioserver.

To provide exact per-daemon isolation, SystemMemoryBudgetManager writes protection across all three levels of the cgroup v2 hierarchy on every refresh, as shown in figure 1:

  1. Leaf process node (pid_<pid>/memory.min): Set to the process's (scaled) 90% working-set floor.
  2. UID node (uid_<uid>/memory.min): Set to the exact sum of its managed pid_* leaf floors, so unmanaged processes sharing that UID (such as other AID_SYSTEM daemons or sharedUserId="android.uid.system" packages) have memory.min = 0 and can't claim protection.
  3. Top-level slice (/sys/fs/cgroup/system/memory.min and /sys/fs/cgroup/apps/memory.min): Set to the exact sum of its uid_* children. Any stale memory.low values on managed nodes are cleared to 0, and any uid_* directories that were managed on a previous refresh (such as a previous Home launcher after the user switches launchers) are reset to 0.

Figure 1. Three-level protection floor delegation across cgroup slices.

Why memory.min is used instead of memory.low on MGLRU kernels

Under Multi-Generational LRU (MGLRU, the default page reclaim engine on Android 6.6 and newer kernels), memory.low and memory.min behave differently in mm/vmscan.c:shrink_one:

  • memory.low (single-pass deferral): A cgroup whose usage is under memory.low is rotated to the tail of the memcg LRU (MEMCG_LRU_TAIL) and skipped for a single reclaim pass. On the next pass under sustained memory pressure, the kernel reclaims the cgroup in full and logs a MEMCG_LOW event. In physical-device stress tests with an anonymous memory hog growing to 85% of physical RAM, memory.low allowed SystemUI on a smartwatch to collapse from ~45 MB down to ~5 to 10 MB and audioserver on a 16 GB foldable to drop from 15 MB to 2 MB against a ~14 MB floor.
  • memory.min (hard protection floor): A cgroup whose usage is under memory.min is skipped by global reclaim. As shown in figure 2, under the same 85% RAM pressure workload, memory.min sheds only the coldest 10% tail of each daemon and holds SystemUI, surfaceflinger, and audioserver at their 90% floors with zero anonymous refaults and no increase in lmkd process terminations.

memory.min provides a hard physical reservation matching the protection of the PinnerService mlock pinning it replaces, with the advantage that the kernel LRU (rather than a static file list) chooses which hot code, heap, and graphics pages stay resident.

Figure 2. Daemon working-set retention under rising memory pressure.

Boot prewarming and post-boot unmapped file cache reclaim

Replacing the PinnerService permanent mlock of config_defaultPinnerServiceFiles requires coordinating two boot-time behaviors:

  • One-shot background boot prewarming (PinnerService): Skipping PinnerService mlock without warming the page cache shifts ~95 MB of SystemUI APK, ODEX, and VDEX disk reads onto the synchronous boot path when SystemUI starts (OnBootPhase_550), adding 300 to 450 ms to boot completion. Calling madvise(MADV_WILLNEED) isn't sufficient because force_page_cache_ra in the kernel clamps a single MADV_WILLNEED call to one readahead window (typically 128 KB to 2 MB). Instead, when SystemMemoryBudgetManager.shouldSkipDefaultSystemPinning is active, PinnerService maps each file in config_defaultPinnerServiceFiles on a background thread during onStart, synchronously populates the file into the page cache with Os.mlock, and immediately calls Os.munlock, munmap, and close. This preserves fast boot timing while leaving zero permanently locked bytes so cold startup pages can be evicted later.
  • Excluding unmapped file cache and reclaiming boot package-scan cache: During boot, PackageManagerService scans installed APKs, leaving 1.5 to 2.5 GB of cold unmapped file page cache charged to the system_server cgroup, and other protected processes (such as SystemUI reading 3D asset files on XR devices) can also retain unmapped file cache from one-time reads. If included in the memory.min calculation, that cold cache can saturate the 10% global RAM cap and proportionally scale down the protection floors of surfaceflinger, SystemUI, and audioserver. To prevent cap starvation, SystemMemoryBudgetManager reads memory.stat for each protected process, computes unmapped file cache as max(0, file - shmem - file_mapped), and subtracts that unmapped cache from memory.current before computing the 90% floor, as shown in figure 3. In addition, 10 seconds after PHASE_BOOT_COMPLETED, the manager performs a one-shot write of <unmapped_file> swappiness=0 to the memory.reclaim node of system_server on Linux 6.2 and newer kernels to proactively evict cold package-scan cache without swapping anonymous heap or evicting mapped DEX and code pages. On older kernels (such as android14-6.1) that reject swappiness=0 with EINVAL, the manager skips the memory.reclaim write rather than falling back to an unqualified reclaim write that would swap out anonymous heap during boot.

Figure 3. Protection floor convergence and cache reclaim after boot.

Kernel requirements and device configuration overlays

SystemMemoryBudgetManager relies on mem_cgroup_calculate_protection in the Linux kernel to propagate memory.min across nested cgroups. Android common kernels android15-6.6 and android16-6.12 include full MGLRU nested protection support out of the box. Devices running android14-6.1 with MGLRU enabled require three upstream backports in mm/vmscan.c and mm/memcontrol.c so empty intermediate slice and UID cgroups propagate protection to leaf process cgroups:

  • 30d77b7eef01 (mm/mglru: fix ineffective protection calculation)
  • 8aa420617918 (mm/mglru: respect min_ttl_ms with memcgs)
  • adb8213014b2 (mm: memcg: fix stale protection of reclaim target memcg)

OEMs can enable, customize, or disable SystemMemoryBudgetManager using the following feature flag and framework resource overlays:

  • com.android.server.am.system_process_memory_budgets (aconfig feature flag): Enables SystemMemoryBudgetManager and skips default PinnerService system and Home mlock pinning (disabled by default in the initial Android 17 release).
  • config_systemMemoryBudgetLowKb (integer, KB): 0 (default) caps the sum of all memory.min floors at 10% of total physical RAM. A positive value sets an explicit cap in KB, and a negative value disables SystemMemoryBudgetManager on the device (retaining legacy PinnerService static mlock pinning).
  • config_systemMemoryBudgetHighKb (integer, KB): 0 (default) leaves /sys/fs/cgroup/system/memory.high at max. A positive value sets a top slice memory.high ceiling (must be greater than or equal to the floor cap).

  • config_systemMemoryBudgetAdditionalSystemProcesses (string-array): Lists additional latency-critical native system or vendor daemon process names in /sys/fs/cgroup/system (matched against /proc/<pid>/comm or the basename of argv[0] in /proc/<pid>/cmdline for system and vendor UIDs under 10000) to protect with 90% memory.min floors alongside the default six system daemons. Use this overlay rather than setting memory.min in init.rc because SystemMemoryBudgetManager recomputes uid_<uid>/memory.min as the sum of its managed leaf processes and clears unmanaged uid_* nodes on every refresh. For example, an XR device can protect its spatial tracking and camera HAL daemons (android.hardware.perceptionhost and auracamerahal), and an Android Desktop device can protect its audio and USB camera HAL daemons (dras.core.audio and android.hardware.camera.provider-usb-service.android-desktop):

    <!-- XR device overlay -->
<string-array translatable="false" name="config_systemMemoryBudgetAdditionalSystemProcesses">
    <item>android.hardware.perceptionhost</item>
    <item>auracamerahal</item>
</string-array>

<!-- Android Desktop device overlay -->
<string-array translatable="false" name="config_systemMemoryBudgetAdditionalSystemProcesses">
    <item>dras.core.audio</item>
    <item>android.hardware.camera.provider-usb-service.android-desktop</item>
</string-array>

  • config_systemUi (string): Package name of the platform SystemUI app, resolved with MATCH_SYSTEM_ONLY.

To inspect active SystemMemoryBudgetManager floors and cgroup nodes on a device, run:

# Inspect policy state, resolved PIDs, and applied floors
adb shell dumpsys system_server_dumper --name SystemMemoryBudgetManager
adb shell dumpsys meminfo | sed -n '/System Memory Budgets/,$p'
# Inspect raw cgroup v2 memory.min nodes across the system and apps slices
adb shell head -n 1 \
  /sys/fs/cgroup/system/memory.min \
  /sys/fs/cgroup/system/uid_*/memory.min \
  /sys/fs/cgroup/system/uid_*/pid_*/memory.min \
  /sys/fs/cgroup/apps/memory.min \
  /sys/fs/cgroup/apps/uid_*/memory.min \
  /sys/fs/cgroup/apps/uid_*/pid_*/memory.min

Bound persistent and background system apps with memory budgets

While SystemMemoryBudgetManager protects interactive daemons from reclaim using memory.min floors, many other system apps and privileged platform services run in the background for long periods as PERSISTENT processes, bound foreground services, or frequently queried content providers. Without explicit memory ceilings, these processes aren't constrained until they reach multi-gigabyte Memory Limiter limits (such as 4 GB to 10 GB for visible apps and 2 GB to 5 GB for background apps) or global memory pressure triggers system-wide kswapd and low-memory killer (lmkd) activity.

Left unconstrained, background system processes often accumulate large amounts of cold memory that isn't part of their active working set:

  • Unbounded file page cache: Services that index media, search databases, or sync calendar and provider tables (such as AppSearch, MediaProvider, and CalendarProvider) map or stream through large files on disk. Without a cgroup memory.high ceiling, clean file-backed pages from one-time reads remain charged to the process cgroup indefinitely, consuming hundreds of megabytes of physical RAM.
  • Post-burst anonymous heap retention: Services that experience transient activity spikes, such as Bluetooth audio and BLE discovery bursts, NetworkStack captive-portal TLS validation, or UI helpers transitioning to the background, can retain cold anonymous heap pages long after the burst completes.

Applying calibrated <memory-budget> declarations (memory.high soft limits, typically 30 MB to 190 MB) to system apps provides two primary benefits:

  • Proactive, localized page reclaim: When a system process crosses its configured memory.high budget, the Linux kernel directs page reclaim specifically at that cgroup, evicting cold file-backed pages first and compressing inactive anonymous pages to ZRAM without waiting for global device memory pressure.
  • More available RAM for foreground apps and the cached app pool: Bounding cold file caches across always-on system services reclaims tens to hundreds of megabytes of physical RAM across the device, reducing UI jank, lowering camera launch pressure, and keeping more user apps alive in the cached state.

Configure system app memory budgets

System apps use the same <memory-budget> manifest syntax, process-state cascading, display-density scaling, and last-matching-clause resolution rule as general apps. For the full list of attributes, see the XML attribute reference.

OEMs can declare <memory-budget> elements directly inside a system app's AndroidManifest.xml or merge them from a separate XML file using the additional_manifests property in Android.bp. By convention, AOSP stores reference system app budgets in standalone *-budget.xml files (either in frameworks/base/core/memory_budgets/ for core platform packages or alongside individual modules such as packages/modules/NetworkStack/memory_budgets/, packages/modules/AppSearch/apk/, and packages/services/Telephony/) and attaches them with additional_manifests:

android_app {
    name: "TeleService",
    manifest: "AndroidManifest.xml",
    additional_manifests: ["Telephony-budget.xml"],
    // ...
}
Important: If you merge a budget file using additional_manifests, always include <uses-sdk android:targetSdkVersion="10000" /> at the top of the budget XML file. In Soong builds, only the primary AndroidManifest.xml passes through ManifestFixer to inject the platform targetSdkVersion. Files listed in additional_manifests are passed to manifest-merger as library manifests. Without <uses-sdk>, manifest-merger defaults to targetSdkVersion="1" and injects legacy compatibility permissions (READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE, WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE, and READ_PHONE_STATE) into the merged APK.

Package-level (UID) versus process-level (PID) scoping

Whether you declare a package-level baseline budget (<application>) or a multi-process budget (<processes><process>) determines whether the kernel enforces memory.high at the UID cgroup level (/sys/fs/cgroup/uid_<uid>/memory.high) or at the per-PID cgroup level (/sys/fs/cgroup/uid_<uid>/pid_<pid>/memory.high), as shown in figure 4:

  • Package-level (<application>) budget: Use when the APK runs a single process under its own dedicated UID (for example, Bluetooth, Nfc, NetworkStack, CalendarProvider, Traceur, or AppSearch).
  • Process-level (<processes><process>) budget: Use when the APK shares android:sharedUserId (such as android.uid.phone with UID 1001 or android.uid.system with UID 1000) with other system packages so other processes sharing that UID aren't throttled together, or when a single APK runs multiple processes with distinct memory roles (for example, the background MediaProvider daemon and the :PhotoPicker UI subprocess).

Figure 4. UID-level versus PID-level memory ceilings.

The following example shows MediaProvider-budget.xml, which scopes RAM-tiered budgets to the default MediaProvider process (<process>) and a display-scaled budget to the :PhotoPicker UI process. Each android:maxDeviceRamMb attribute matches devices whose total physical RAM (MemTotal) is at or below the specified MB threshold (or applies to any RAM capacity when omitted). Clauses are ordered from the unconstrained default down to the smallest maxDeviceRamMb threshold so the last-matching-clause resolution rule selects the tightest applicable tier:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<manifest xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
          package="com.android.providers.media.module">
    <uses-sdk android:targetSdkVersion="10000" />
    <application>
        <processes>
            <process>
                <memory-budget
                    android:maxMb="85" />
                <memory-budget
                    android:maxMb="75"
                    android:maxDeviceRamMb="12288" />
                <memory-budget
                    android:maxMb="60"
                    android:maxDeviceRamMb="8192" />
            </process>
            <process android:process=":PhotoPicker">
                <memory-budget
                    android:maxMb="85"
                    android:additionalBytesPerDisplayPixel="25" />
            </process>
        </processes>
    </application>
</manifest>

When you declare <processes> in a budget manifest, list <process> entries only for the processes that declare a <memory-budget> (if the default app process declares a custom android:process name on <application>, specify that name on its <process android:process="..."> element rather than using an unnamed <process /> tag). During APK compilation, aapt2 automatically adds <process> entries for any unbudgeted processes declared by components in the merged manifest and, when needed for compatibility with Android 17, inserts an enclosing <memory-budget android:maxMb="1000000" /> under <application> so per-process budgets stay isolated to their target processes.

Note: If you build a multi-process budget manifest with an older aapt2 binary for an Android 17 system image that predates the aapt2 and MemoryLimiter per-process isolation fixes, include an enclosing <memory-budget android:maxMb="1000000" /> directly under <application> and list a <process> entry for every process in the merged manifest.

How AOSP reference budgets were calibrated on Google Pixel devices

The reference system app memory budgets in AOSP were calibrated across Google Pixel devices sweeping 6 GB to 16 GB of physical RAM (including 6 GB, 8 GB, 12 GB, and 16 GB phones, foldables, and tablets) and display resolutions ranging from ~1.2 MP (720×1600) to ~4.5 MP (2076×2152).

Calibration combined two complementary data sources: fleet-wide cgroup v2 field telemetry and controlled physical-device memory.high sweeps across critical user journeys (CUJs).

Fleet-wide cgroup v2 telemetry analysis

Periodic cgroup v2 snapshots were collected across the device fleet and sliced by physical RAM tier (≤8 GB, 12 GB, and ≥16 GB) and process state bucket (foreground, perceptible, background, and cached). Six principles guided the statistical analysis:

  • Decompose memory.current into working set versus reclaimable file cache: Because memory.high governs resident cgroup charge (memory.current), each snapshot was decomposed using memory.stat into anonymous heap (anon), swapped anonymous pages (swap), and file-backed page cache (file), as shown in figure 5. Total incompressible anonymous demand (anon + swap at P99) establishes the minimum working-set floor for the budget so the process doesn't risk ZRAM exhaustion, while a large gap between memory.current P99 and anon + swap P99 indicates file page cache that memory.high can reclaim, provided that cache is unmapped and cold.
  • Account for memory that memory.high can't reclaim: Not all file and shared memory is cold cache. Pages that are locked (unevictable in memory.stat, such as shared memory locked with mlock or the locked guest RAM of a virtual machine whose host processes are charged to the app's cgroup) set a hard floor under the budget, and mapped pages (file_mapped) are often part of the active working set. Check unevictable, shmem, and file_mapped before treating file memory as reclaimable. For example, about 100 MB of AppSearch memory is locked and unevictable, so its budget covers that floor plus its hot host working set, with headroom for the locked region to grow.
  • Filter out idle-state dilution: Content providers (CalendarProvider) and on-demand developer tools (Traceur) spend 70% to 99.9% of field snapshots idle at ~1 MB to 3 MB. Computing raw percentiles across all snapshots severely dilutes P95 and P99 estimates. Instead, percentiles and confidence intervals were computed over undiluted active snapshots (filtering out CACHED snapshots and idle baseline snapshots).
  • Use device-clustered confidence intervals: Because a single device contributes many periodic snapshots over time, treating snapshots as independent samples understates tail uncertainty. All P95 and P99 working set estimates were evaluated using conservative device-clustered 95% confidence intervals (using the distinct device count N_dev as the effective sample size).
  • Account for transient bursts with memory.peak: Periodic sampling can miss short-lived, high-allocation bursts (such as NetworkStack captive-portal TLS validation and concurrent DNS probes, or Bluetooth A2DP and BLE initialization). For bursty services, budgets were sized to cover the 90th to 95th percentile of lifetime kernel memory.peak high-water marks across RAM tiers.
  • Confirm that a RAM tier reflects RAM, not device generation: Newer devices tend to have both more RAM and more features, so a working set that grows with RAM tier might actually be growing with features. Before adding a maxDeviceRamMb tier, slice the data by device model. For example, com.android.phone reaches the same P99 anon + swap (~85 to 90 MB) on 12 GB and 16 GB phones of the same generation, while an older 12 GB foldable uses 40 MB. Its budget therefore uses a single value with no RAM tier, so that a lower-RAM device that ships the newer telephony features isn't under-budgeted.

Figure 5. Working set versus reclaimable file cache.

Physical-device CUJ and display-scaling sweeps

To validate the telemetry-derived budgets and calibrate display-proportional budgets (such as :PhotoPicker) and state-specific background budgets (such as Traceur), live memory.high sweeps were executed on physical devices spanning 6 GB to 16 GB RAM:

  • Finding the zero-refault knee: While driving end-to-end CUJs (such as fast photo grid flinging, album browsing, full-screen high-resolution photo and video preview swiping, and trace recording and saving), memory.high was stepped downward while measuring cgroup memory.stat counters (workingset_refault_anon, workingset_refault_file, pgscan, and pgsteal) and memory.events (high). As illustrated in figure 6, the optimal budget sits just over the zero-refault knee. The zero-refault knee is the threshold where the kernel reclaims cold one-time file cache (pgsteal > 0) without triggering active working-set thrashing (workingset_refault == 0).
  • Validating display-pixel scaling across resolutions: Testing :PhotoPicker across four physical and emulated display resolutions from ~1.2 MP (720×1600) to ~4.5 MP (2076×2152 unfolded inner display) confirmed that its active Glide and ViewPager2 bitmap working set scales linearly with display pixel count. The non-display baseline also varies by device: at nearly the same pixel count, the zero-refault knee was about 140 MB on a 16 GB foldable's outer display versus 110 to 125 MB on a 6 GB phone. An 85 MB baseline plus 25 bytes per display pixel (android:maxMb="85" and android:additionalBytesPerDisplayPixel="25") stays above the measured knee on every tested display (~110 MB on HD+, ~145 MB on FHD+, and ~190 MB on unfolded displays).
  • Verifying ART garbage collection in background states: In cgroup v2, Zygote-shared boot.art and framework image pages remain charged to Zygote's cgroup and are treated as an immune space during ART concurrent mark-compact (CMC) garbage collection. Stress testing confirmed that when a system UI app transitions to background, tightening memory.high (for example, to 30 MB on Traceur) cleanly bounds private heap and page cache without causing GC thrashing or swap activity.

Figure 6. Finding the zero-refault knee during a CUJ.

Summary of AOSP reference system app budgets

The following table summarizes the calibrated reference budgets in AOSP across RAM tiers and process states:

How OEMs can recalibrate system app budgets for their own devices

OEMs that customize system apps (for example, adding vendor Bluetooth profiles, custom telephony extensions, or OEM media indexers) or ship additional preinstalled system services can recalibrate existing budgets or author new *-budget.xml files for their hardware portfolio.

Collect active cgroup v2 memory profiles

For each target system process, read its cgroup v2 memory nodes under /sys/fs/cgroup/uid_<uid>/pid_<pid>/ across representative workloads and RAM tiers:

  • memory.current: Current resident memory charged to the cgroup (excluding Zygote-shared pages)
  • memory.peak: Lifetime peak memory.current high-water mark since process start
  • memory.swap.current: Current compressed swap usage in ZRAM
  • memory.stat: Breakdown of anon, file, pgscan, pgsteal, workingset_refault_anon, and workingset_refault_file
  • memory.events: Cumulative count of high breaches (memory.high throttling and reclaim events)

When aggregating telemetry from dogfood or field devices, separate active process states (TOP, FOREGROUND_SERVICE, active bindings, and active syncs) from idle CACHED or idle PERSISTENT states so idle snapshots don't skew your P95 and P99 working-set calculations downward.

Separate incompressible heap from reclaimable file cache

Compare the 99th percentile of anon + swap against the 99th percentile of memory.current:

  • File-cache-dominated services (file ≫ anon, such as database providers, search indexers, and log daemons): Set android:maxMb to provide comfortable headroom (typically 1.5x to 4x) over P99 anon + swap plus a working window for hot file pages. This configuration lets the kernel continuously evict cold unmapped file pages without touching anonymous heap. If unevictable or file_mapped is large (as with locked memory or memory-mapped databases), count that footprint as working set too.
  • Anonymous-heap-dominated or bursty services (anon makes up most of memory.current, such as networking or connectivity stacks): Size android:maxMb to cover P90 to P95 of memory.peak so transient bursts don't trigger synchronous ZRAM swap-out on latency-sensitive threads.
  • Display-intensive UI processes (such as pickers, galleries, or system UI helpers): Measure the baseline non-UI footprint and the incremental bitmap footprint per megapixel across your lowest- and highest-resolution displays, and express the budget using android:maxMb plus android:additionalBytesPerDisplayPixel.

Sweep memory.high on physical devices

Before committing a new budget to the build, use am memory-limiter manual (or write directly to the process's memory.high cgroup node on a userdebug build) to test candidate limits while running your automated CUJ tests:

# Override memory.high for a specific PID to 60 MB during a CUJ test
adb shell am memory-limiter manual <PID> 60MB

Monitor memory.stat and memory.events before and after the CUJ:

  • Budget is too low: workingset_refault_anon or workingset_refault_file spikes sharply during the CUJ, memory.swap.current grows continuously during active foreground work, or CUJ frame or Binder latency regresses. Increase the budget past the refault knee.
  • Budget is too high: memory.events:high remains 0 even after heavy file-streaming or indexing workloads, and file in memory.stat grows unboundedly with cold pages. Tighten the budget toward the active working set.
  • Budget is well-calibrated: Steady-state memory.current stays under memory.high during normal operation. During heavy file or cache bursts, pgsteal reclaims cold file pages while workingset_refault_anon remains near zero and CUJ latency is unchanged.
